Front matter

A from-zero guidebook

The RFSoC 4x2 for Semiconductor Spin Qubits

Quantum dots, spin qubits, signals, FPGAs, PYNQ and QICK, explained from the inside out

This book is written for someone who has undergraduate physics, maths and solid-state physics, and who is new to FPGAs, software-defined radio, PYNQ, QICK and to how a quantum-dot or spin-qubit lab actually works. It starts from the beginning of each topic and builds up until you can design, run and understand the experiments that research groups run on Si/SiGe and GaAs quantum-dot devices, and see exactly which parts of that work an RFSoC 4x2 board can do.

Use the contents list on the left (or the Contents button on a phone) to move between chapters. The search box finds section headings and defined terms. Every chapter ends with links to the previous and next chapter.

Part 0 · Orientation · Chapter 1

The big picture: from one electron to a Python notebook

Why you need this

Before learning any single topic in depth, you need a mental map of the whole experiment: what the device is, why it sits in a refrigerator colder than outer space, what kinds of electrical signals it needs, which instrument makes each signal, and where the RFSoC 4x2 fits. Every later chapter zooms into one box of the map drawn here. If you ever feel lost later, come back to Figure 1.1.

A spin-qubit experiment is, at its heart, a conversation between a computer and a single electron. The computer sends carefully timed voltages and microwaves down wires into a refrigerator. Those signals move the electron around, rotate its spin, and then ask it a question: "is your spin up or down?" The answer comes back as a tiny change in an electrical signal, which is amplified, digitised and analysed. This chapter walks through that conversation once, end to end, in plain language.

1.1What the lab is trying to do

A qubit is a physical object with two distinguishable quantum states, which we call \(\ket{0}\) and \(\ket{1}\). Unlike a classical bit, it can also be in a superposition of both. Chapter 2 explains what that means precisely. For now, think of it like this: a classical bit is a switch that is either off or on. A qubit is more like an arrow that can point in any direction on a sphere, where "north" means \(\ket{0}\) and "south" means \(\ket{1}\).

Many physical systems can play this role: superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, defects in diamond, photons, and the system this book is about, the spin of an electron (or hole) trapped in a semiconductor quantum dot. An electron has an intrinsic angular momentum called spin. In a magnetic field its two spin states, "up" and "down", have slightly different energies, and that pair of states is a natural qubit. This idea was proposed by Daniel Loss and David DiVincenzo in 1998 and is now called the Loss–DiVincenzo or single-spin qubit [6].

Why semiconductors? Three reasons dominate the research literature [7, 8]:

  • Size. A quantum dot is about 50–100 nm across. Billions could fit on a chip, much like transistors.
  • Manufacturing. Silicon spin qubits are made with processes close to those that make computer chips, so the semiconductor industry's know-how can, in principle, be reused.
  • Coherence. In isotopically purified silicon (28Si), the electron's spin is very well isolated from its surroundings, so its quantum state survives a long time compared with how fast we can manipulate it.

The lab's job is to build such devices, cool them down, find the right voltages to trap exactly one or a few electrons, and then demonstrate and improve the basic operations: preparing a known state, rotating the spin (single-qubit gates), coupling two spins (two-qubit gates), and measuring the spin (readout). Everything else in this book serves those four tasks.

1.2The device: a chip with gates on top

Figure 1.1 shows a simplified cross-section of a Si/SiGe quantum-dot device, the platform you will use. Read it from the bottom up:

  1. Substrate and buffer. Germanium atoms are slightly larger than silicon atoms. A thick, graded SiGe layer slowly changes the lattice spacing so that the top layers grow as a nearly perfect crystal.
  2. The quantum well. A thin (about 10 nm) layer of pure silicon is sandwiched between SiGe layers. Because of how the conduction band energies line up (Chapter 6), electrons prefer to sit in this silicon layer. They can move freely in the plane but not up or down, so they form a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG).
  3. Spacer and oxide. A SiGe spacer keeps the electrons away from the messy surface, and a thin oxide insulates the gates from the semiconductor.
  4. Gates. Metal electrodes, a few tens of nanometres wide, sit on top. A voltage on a gate changes the electrostatic potential underneath it. Positive voltage attracts electrons, negative repels them. With the right combination of voltages you carve the 2DEG into tiny islands (dots) that each hold a controlled number of electrons, typically one.
  5. Micromagnet. A small ferromagnet (often cobalt) on top of the device. Chapter 12 explains why its non-uniform stray field is so useful.

GaAs devices look similar but use a GaAs/AlGaAs interface instead of a Si quantum well. In GaAs the 2DEG often forms by itself (thanks to doping) and the gates are negative, pushing electrons away to define dots. Chapter 6 compares the two materials, including why GaAs spins lose their coherence faster (nuclear spins) and why silicon has an extra complication called valleys.

1.3Why the device must be so cold

The energies involved are tiny. The energy needed to add one more electron to a dot (the charging energy) is a few milli-electronvolts (meV). The energy difference between spin up and spin down in a 1 T field is about 0.1 meV. Thermal energy at temperature \(T\) is about \(k_B T\), where \(k_B = 86\ \mu\text{eV/K}\) is Boltzmann's constant. At room temperature (300 K), \(k_B T \approx 26\) meV, far larger than all of these energies, so thermal jiggling would wash everything out.

Worked example

What temperature makes thermal energy 10 times smaller than the spin splitting at 0.5 T?

The spin splitting is \(E_Z = g \mu_B B\), with \(g \approx 2\) for electrons in silicon and \(\mu_B = 57.9\ \mu\text{eV/T}\) (the Bohr magneton). At \(B = 0.5\) T: \(E_Z = 2 \times 57.9 \times 0.5 = 57.9\ \mu\text{eV}\). We want \(k_B T = E_Z / 10 = 5.8\ \mu\text{eV}\), so \(T = 5.8 / 86 \approx 0.067\) K = 67 mK.

That is why spin-qubit devices sit in a dilution refrigerator, whose coldest stage (the mixing chamber) reaches about 10 mK. The electrons themselves usually end up somewhat hotter (often 50–150 mK) because of electrical noise coming down the wires. Chapter 16 explains how the wiring is designed to minimise this.

Interestingly, there is a strong research push towards running silicon spin qubits at 1 K or above ("hot qubits"), where much more cooling power is available. The physics is the same; the trade-offs are discussed in Chapter 16.

1.4The signals an experiment needs

Every experiment in this book is built from a small set of signal types. Learning to recognise them is the single most useful skill for understanding what any piece of lab equipment, including the RFSoC, is for.

SignalWhat it doesTypical size and speedTraditional instrument
DC gate voltagesForm the dots: set how many electrons each dot holds and how strongly they couple0 to ±2 V (or more), set to µV precision, changed slowly (ms–s); 10–100 gatesMulti-channel low-noise DC source (e.g. QDevil QDAC, Basel LNHR DAC)
Fast gate pulses ("baseband")Move electrons between charge states within nanoseconds; turn exchange on/off; select readout and load points1–100 mV at the device, rise times ~1 ns, lengths ns to ms, on a few to tens of gatesArbitrary waveform generator (AWG)
Microwave driveRotate the spin (ESR or EDSR)Carrier 1–40 GHz (set by the magnetic field), bursts of ns to µs, precise phaseVector microwave source + IQ modulation from an AWG
Readout stimulus and responseMeasure the charge sensor quicklyRF reflectometry: a carrier of about 100 MHz–1 GHz; or a low-frequency AC excitation (kHz–MHz); response is µV–mV after amplificationRF source + demodulator/digitiser, or a lock-in amplifier
Triggers and markersKeep all instruments in stepDigital 0/3.3 V edges with ns timingAWG marker outputs, pulse generators
Magnetic fieldSplits spin up/down; sets the spin resonance frequency0.1–2 T, very stable, changed rarelySuperconducting magnet + current supply

A well-equipped spin-qubit lab traditionally fills a rack with separate instruments for these jobs: DC sources, AWGs, microwave sources with IQ mixers, lock-in amplifiers, fast digitisers, and a computer that tries to keep them all synchronised. Commercial integrated controllers from companies such as Quantum Machines, Zurich Instruments, Qblox and Keysight combine several of these functions into one system, at a price of tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars. Chapter 17 takes the rack apart box by box.

1.5Where the RFSoC 4x2 fits

The RFSoC (Radio-Frequency System-on-Chip) is a single chip made by AMD (formerly Xilinx) that contains four things that used to be separate:

  1. Fast DACs (digital-to-analog converters) that turn numbers into voltages billions of times per second. On the 4x2 they run at up to 9.85 billion samples per second (GSPS).
  2. Fast ADCs (analog-to-digital converters) that turn voltages into numbers, up to 5 GSPS on this chip.
  3. FPGA fabric: millions of programmable logic elements that can be wired into custom digital circuits, for example a circuit that generates a pulse with nanosecond timing, or one that demodulates a readout signal in real time.
  4. ARM processors that run Linux, so the board is a small computer you can talk to over Ethernet.

Originally designed for 5G base stations and radar, this combination turns out to be very close to what a qubit controller needs. The QICK project (Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit), started at Fermilab and Princeton, provides open-source firmware and Python software that turn an RFSoC board into a qubit controller [9, 3]. HRL Laboratories has published spinQICK, an extension of QICK made specifically for gate-defined spin qubits [10], and demonstrated full control of an exchange-only qubit with it in October 2026 [11].

Here is how one "shot" of a typical spin-qubit experiment flows through Figure 1.1:

  1. You write a short Python program in a Jupyter notebook. With QICK it might say: "pulse gate P1 to −5 mV for 1 µs (initialise), apply a 20 ns microwave burst at 5.2 GHz (rotate the spin), pulse P1 to the readout point and record the sensor signal for 2 µs; repeat 10 000 times."
  2. The QICK library compiles this into a program for the tProcessor, a small processor built in the FPGA fabric that executes commands at precise clock ticks, and sends it to the board over Ethernet.
  3. The tProcessor tells the signal generators exactly when to start. The generators compute waveform samples and feed them to the DACs at 9.8 GSPS.
  4. Analog signals leave the SMA connectors, pass through room-temperature electronics and down the fridge lines to the device.
  5. The electron responds. Its spin state is converted into a charge state (Chapter 11), which changes the conductance of a nearby charge sensor, which changes the readout signal reflected back up the fridge.
  6. The ADC samples the returning signal. FPGA logic multiplies it by a reference sine wave, filters and adds up the result, so that each shot gives just two numbers, I and Q (Chapter 23).
  7. After all repetitions the averaged or single-shot I/Q values are sent back to the PC, where you plot them, fit them and decide what to change.

1.6What the 4x2 can and cannot do, at a glance

The details fill Chapters 28–30 and 45, but you should know the headline facts now so that nothing surprises you later. They come from the board's documentation [1, 2] and the QICK firmware for this board [3].

FeatureRFSoC 4x2What it means for spin qubits
Analog outputs2 DACs on SMA connectors, 14-bit, up to 9.85 GSPS (QICK uses 9.8304 GSPS)Two independent fast output channels. Enough for readout plus one drive or gate, not for a full multi-gate device.
Analog inputs4 ADCs on SMA, 14-bit, up to 5 GSPS (QICK uses 4.42368 GSPS); QICK standard firmware reads 2 of themPlenty for reading charge sensors.
CouplingEvery SMA port passes through capacitors and a balun rated 10 MHz–10 GHzNo DC and no slow signals. Long flat gate pulses droop. Baseband gate pulsing needs either hardware modification or a different board.
Frequency rangeDirect synthesis up to about 6 GHz analog bandwidthReflectometry (100 MHz–1 GHz) is easy. EDSR at low fields (a few GHz) is direct; higher frequencies need an external mixer.
Real-time logicFPGA + QICK tProcessor with conditional branchingFeedback, active reset, real-time averaging, fast 2D scans.
Digital I/O2 PMOD headers (QICK uses 8 outputs as triggers)Trigger DC sources, scopes, other instruments.
Price$2,499 academic (2026), universities and research institutes onlyFar cheaper than commercial qubit controllers.
On the 4x2

The most important single fact for your work is the third row. Spin qubits in gate-defined dots are controlled mostly by baseband gate voltages, meaning pulses that start and end at a DC level, last anything from nanoseconds to milliseconds, and have no carrier frequency. The 4x2's outputs are transformer-coupled and AC-coupled, so they cannot hold a DC level. The experiments that used RFSoCs on spin qubits so far all used the larger ZCU216 board with DC-coupled amplifiers [11, 10]. With the 4x2 you can still do a great deal: RF reflectometry readout, microwave EDSR drive, fast charge-stability maps using AC-coupled tricks, single-shot readout analysis and real-time feedback. Baseband pulsing needs extra hardware, discussed honestly in Chapters 29 and 38.

1.7The software stack, from top to bottom

Several layers of software and firmware sit between your notebook and the DAC pins. You will meet each in its own chapter, so here is the list:

  1. Jupyter notebook: an interactive Python document in your browser (Chapter 31).
  2. Your experiment code: Python classes describing pulse sequences, sweeps and analysis. With spinQICK, many standard spin-qubit experiments are already written.
  3. QICK Python library: translates your pulse sequence into tProcessor machine code, configures generators and readouts, and collects data (Chapters 33–35).
  4. PYNQ: AMD's Python framework that loads FPGA designs ("overlays") and gives Python access to their registers and memories (Chapters 31–32).
  5. Linux on the ARM cores.
  6. The bitstream: the file that configures the FPGA fabric into QICK's circuits (Chapter 27).
  7. The RF data converters: hard-wired DAC and ADC blocks on the chip, configured by the bitstream and by Python (Chapter 26).
Analogy

Think of the RFSoC as an orchestra. The ARM CPU is the manager who talks to the outside world (you) and hands out the sheet music. The tProcessor in the FPGA is the conductor who keeps perfect time. The signal generators are the musicians who play the notes, and the DACs are their instruments. The ADCs and readout blocks are the recording engineers. QICK is the arrangement that tells everyone their part. PYNQ is the stage crew who set up the hall.

1.8How the rest of the book is organised

The book climbs from physics to hardware to experiments:

  • Part I (Chapters 2–5) builds the quantum mechanics of a two-level system: states, rotations, decoherence and measurement. This is the language every qubit paper uses.
  • Parts II and III (Chapters 6–15) are the heart of the physics: how quantum dots form, how we see single electrons, how spin qubits of every kind (single-spin, singlet–triplet, exchange-only and others) are made, controlled and read out, and how a real device is tuned.
  • Part IV (Chapters 16–17) tours the lab: refrigerator, wiring and instruments.
  • Parts V and VI (Chapters 18–27) teach signals, sampling, I/Q, digital signal processing, FPGAs and the RFSoC chip, following and extending AMD's SDR book [5].
  • Parts VII–IX (Chapters 28–37) cover the 4x2 board, PYNQ, QICK and spinQICK in depth.
  • Part X (Chapters 38–44) describes each real experiment: what it measures, the pulse sequence, how to run it on the 4x2, what extra hardware is needed, and what good data looks like.
  • Part XI (Chapters 45–46) gives an honest capability map and a step-by-step plan for your own work with the board.
Check yourself

1. Why can't spin-qubit experiments be done at room temperature?

Show answer
Thermal energy \(k_BT\) at 300 K (about 26 meV) is much larger than the charging energy (a few meV) and the spin splitting (about 0.1 meV at 1 T), so thermal excitations would randomise both the electron number and the spin. Cooling to about 10–100 mK makes \(k_BT\) of order 1–10 µeV, well below these energies.

2. Name the four kinds of electrical signal most spin-qubit experiments need, and say which one the 4x2 cannot produce without modification.

Show answer
DC gate voltages, fast baseband gate pulses, microwave drive, and readout stimulus/response (plus triggers). The 4x2 cannot produce DC voltages or long baseband pulses because its outputs are AC-coupled through capacitors and baluns.

3. In one sentence each, what do the DAC, ADC, FPGA fabric and ARM CPU of an RFSoC do in a qubit experiment?

Show answer
The DAC turns computed waveform samples into the analog pulses sent to the device; the ADC digitises the returning readout signal; the FPGA fabric runs the timing processor, waveform generators and real-time demodulation; the ARM CPU runs Linux and Python, receives programs from the PC and returns data.
Summary
  • A spin qubit is the spin of a single electron (or hole) trapped in a gate-defined quantum dot, cooled to millikelvin temperatures in a dilution refrigerator.
  • Experiments need DC gate voltages, fast baseband pulses, microwave drive, readout signals and triggers.
  • An RFSoC combines fast DACs, fast ADCs, FPGA logic and ARM CPUs; QICK and spinQICK turn it into a qubit controller.
  • The 4x2 has 2 outputs and 4 inputs, all AC-coupled (10 MHz–10 GHz baluns). It is excellent for readout and microwave work and needs extra hardware for baseband gate pulsing.

Part I · Quantum mechanics you need · Chapter 2

Two-level systems, states and the Bloch sphere

Why you need this

Every spin-qubit paper describes its experiments in the language of this chapter: states written as \(\ket{\uparrow}\) and \(\ket{\downarrow}\), rotations on the Bloch sphere, "π/2 pulses", "the x axis" and "the phase of the drive". When you later program the RFSoC to play a microwave burst with a certain phase, you are choosing an axis on the Bloch sphere. This chapter gives you that picture precisely, starting from what a quantum state is.

You already know quantum mechanics from undergraduate courses: wavefunctions, the Schrödinger equation, the hydrogen atom. Qubit physics uses a smaller and simpler corner of it. Instead of wavefunctions spread over space, we only care about two states. Everything becomes 2×2 matrices and complex numbers, and the whole state can be drawn as an arrow on a sphere.

2.1From a classical bit to a quantum state

A classical bit is either 0 or 1. If you do not know which, you can describe your knowledge with probabilities, \(p_0\) and \(p_1 = 1 - p_0\), but the bit itself is always in one definite state.

A quantum two-level system is described by a state vector, written in Dirac's "ket" notation as \(\ket{\psi}\). For two levels it is a column of two complex numbers:

\[ \ket{\psi} = a\ket{0} + b\ket{1} = \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \ket{0} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix},\quad \ket{1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

The two states \(\ket{0}\) and \(\ket{1}\) form the computational basis. The numbers \(a\) and \(b\) are complex probability amplitudes. They must satisfy the normalisation condition

\[ |a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1 . \]

For a spin qubit, the two levels are the spin states of one electron along the direction of the static magnetic field. The convention in most spin-qubit papers is that the lower-energy state (spin aligned with the field for an electron with \(g>0\) in the usual sign convention) is \(\ket{\downarrow}\) and labelled \(\ket{0}\), and the higher-energy state is \(\ket{\uparrow} = \ket{1}\). Some papers use the opposite labelling, so always check the definitions in each paper. In this book, \(\ket{0} = \ket{\downarrow}\) (ground state) and \(\ket{1} = \ket{\uparrow}\) (excited state).

Analogy

Think of \(a\) and \(b\) as two arrows in the complex plane, like two clock hands. The length of each hand says how much of that basis state is present. The angle of each hand is its phase. Lengths decide probabilities. The angle between the hands, called the relative phase, has no classical counterpart. It is what makes interference, and therefore quantum computing, possible.

Inner products and what "orthogonal" means

The "bra" \(\bra{\phi}\) is the conjugate transpose of \(\ket{\phi}\): if \(\ket{\phi} = (c, d)^T\) then \(\bra{\phi} = (c^*, d^*)\). The inner product

\[ \braket{\phi}{\psi} = c^* a + d^* b \]

is a complex number that measures how much the two states overlap. Two states are orthogonal when \(\braket{\phi}{\psi} = 0\): they are perfectly distinguishable. \(\ket{0}\) and \(\ket{1}\) are orthogonal. Normalisation is simply \(\braket{\psi}{\psi} = 1\).

2.2Measurement and why we repeat every experiment thousands of times

When you measure a qubit in the computational basis, the result is always either 0 or 1, never something in between. The Born rule gives the probabilities:

\[ P(0) = |\braket{0}{\psi}|^2 = |a|^2, \qquad P(1) = |\braket{1}{\psi}|^2 = |b|^2 . \]

After the measurement, the state is (ideally) the one you observed. A single measurement therefore tells you almost nothing about \(a\) and \(b\). To learn \(P(1)\), you must prepare the same state many times and measure it each time. Each preparation-and-measurement is called a shot.

This has a direct practical consequence for every experiment you will run. If you take \(N\) shots and count \(n\) ones, your estimate of \(P(1)\) is \(\hat P = n/N\). Because each shot is an independent coin flip with probability \(P\), the count follows a binomial distribution and the statistical uncertainty of your estimate is

\[ \sigma_{\hat P} = \sqrt{\frac{P(1-P)}{N}} . \]
Worked example

Your Rabi experiment (Chapter 3) shows \(P(1) \approx 0.5\) in the middle of an oscillation. How many shots per point do you need for an uncertainty of 0.01 (one percentage point)?

\(\sigma = \sqrt{0.5 \times 0.5 / N} = 0.5/\sqrt{N}\). Setting \(0.5/\sqrt N = 0.01\) gives \(\sqrt N = 50\), so \(N = 2500\) shots. If one shot takes 50 µs (initialisation, manipulation and readout), each point takes 0.125 s, and a 100-point sweep takes about 13 s. This kind of estimate tells you how long your experiments will run, which in turn decides how fast your readout must be. It is one reason fast readout (Chapter 9) matters so much.

On the 4x2

The repetition is done in hardware. In QICK you set reps (shots inside one program run) and rounds (how many times the whole program is run). The tProcessor loops over shots without any Python involvement, so a shot can be as short as the physics allows. QICK can return either the average over shots or every single shot's I/Q value, which you then threshold to get 0s and 1s (Chapters 23 and 35).

2.3Global phase, relative phase and the Bloch sphere

Two complex numbers have four real parameters. Normalisation removes one. One more is physically meaningless: multiplying the whole state by a phase factor \(e^{i\gamma}\) changes no probability and no measurable quantity. This global phase can be dropped. That leaves two real parameters, and every pure qubit state can be written as

\[ \ket{\psi} = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\,\ket{0} + e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\,\ket{1}, \qquad 0 \le \theta \le \pi,\quad 0 \le \varphi < 2\pi. \]

The two angles \(\theta\) and \(\varphi\) are exactly the polar and azimuthal angles of a point on a unit sphere. This is the Bloch sphere.

Read the picture like this:

  • Latitude \(\theta\) sets the probabilities. \(P(1) = \sin^2(\theta/2) = (1 - \cos\theta)/2\). At the north pole \(P(1)=0\), at the equator \(P(1) = 1/2\), at the south pole \(P(1) = 1\).
  • Longitude \(\varphi\) is the relative phase. It does not change \(P(0)\) or \(P(1)\), but it changes what happens when you later rotate the state. States on the equator at different \(\varphi\) all give 50/50 results when measured directly, yet they are completely different states: \(\ket{+}\) and \(\ket{-} = (\ket 0 - \ket 1)/\sqrt 2\) are orthogonal.
  • Opposite points are orthogonal states. Note the factor of 1/2 in \(\theta/2\): an angle of 180° on the sphere corresponds to orthogonal states, whose state vectors are 90° apart in the abstract vector space.
Common mistake

People new to qubits often think that "the qubit is 50% in each state" means it is randomly in one or the other, like a classical coin. It does not. \(\ket{+}\) is a single definite state. If you rotate it by 90° about the y axis you get \(\ket{0}\) with certainty, every single time. A random 50/50 classical mixture, rotated the same way, would still give 50/50. The Ramsey experiment in Chapter 4 is exactly a test of this difference, and losing it is what we call dephasing.

2.4Operators, Pauli matrices and the Bloch vector

Physical quantities are represented by Hermitian operators (matrices equal to their own conjugate transpose). For one qubit, every such operator can be built from the identity \(I\) and the three Pauli matrices:

\[ \sigma_x = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \sigma_y = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \sigma_z = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Useful facts you can verify by multiplying matrices: each squares to the identity (\(\sigma_k^2 = I\)); they anticommute (\(\sigma_x\sigma_y = -\sigma_y\sigma_x = i\sigma_z\), and cyclic permutations); and their eigenvalues are \(\pm 1\). The eigenvectors of \(\sigma_z\) are \(\ket 0\) (eigenvalue +1) and \(\ket 1\) (eigenvalue −1); those of \(\sigma_x\) are \(\ket\pm\); those of \(\sigma_y\) are \(\ket{\pm i}\).

For an electron spin, the spin angular momentum operator is \(\vec S = \tfrac{\hbar}{2}\vec\sigma\). So "\(\sigma_z = +1\)" literally means "spin component along z is \(+\hbar/2\)".

The expectation values of the Pauli operators are the Cartesian coordinates of the Bloch vector:

\[ \vec r = \big(\ev{\sigma_x}, \ev{\sigma_y}, \ev{\sigma_z}\big) = (\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta). \]

You can check the z component directly: \(\ev{\sigma_z} = |a|^2 - |b|^2 = \cos^2(\theta/2) - \sin^2(\theta/2) = \cos\theta\). In an experiment, you only ever measure \(\sigma_z\) directly (spin up or down along the field). To measure \(\ev{\sigma_x}\), you first rotate the state by −90° about y, which moves the x axis to the z axis, and then measure. This trick, rotating before measuring, is how state tomography works.

2.5Time evolution: a spin precessing in a magnetic field

The Schrödinger equation \(i\hbar\,\frac{d}{dt}\ket{\psi} = H\ket{\psi}\) tells you how a state changes in time. For a spin in a static field \(B_0\) along z, the Hamiltonian is the Zeeman energy

\[ H_0 = \tfrac{1}{2}\, g\mu_B B_0\, \sigma_z = \tfrac{\hbar\omega_0}{2}\,\sigma_z, \qquad \omega_0 = \frac{g\mu_B B_0}{\hbar}. \]

Here \(g\) is the electron g-factor (about 2.00 in silicon, about −0.44 in GaAs) and \(\mu_B = 9.274\times10^{-24}\) J/T is the Bohr magneton. With the sign conventions above, the energies of the two states differ by \(E_Z = \hbar\omega_0 = |g|\mu_B B_0\), the Zeeman splitting.

Because \(H_0\) is diagonal, the solution is immediate. Starting from \(a\ket0 + b\ket1\):

\[ \ket{\psi(t)} = a\,e^{-i\omega_0 t/2}\ket 0 + b\,e^{+i\omega_0 t/2}\ket 1 \;=\; e^{-i\omega_0 t/2}\big(a\ket 0 + b\,e^{i\omega_0 t}\ket 1\big). \]

Dropping the global phase, the relative phase grows as \(\varphi(t) = \varphi(0) + \omega_0 t\). On the Bloch sphere, the vector keeps its latitude and spins around the z axis at angular frequency \(\omega_0\). This is Larmor precession, and \(f_0 = \omega_0/2\pi\) is the Larmor frequency, which equals the qubit frequency.

Worked example: qubit frequencies

The qubit frequency per tesla is \(f_0/B_0 = |g|\mu_B/h\). With \(\mu_B/h = 13.996\) GHz/T:

  • Silicon, \(g \approx 2.00\): about 28.0 GHz/T. At 0.5 T, \(f_0 \approx 14\) GHz.
  • GaAs, \(|g| \approx 0.44\): about 6.2 GHz/T. At 1 T, \(f_0 \approx 6.2\) GHz.
  • Holes in germanium have strongly anisotropic g-factors (from about 0.1 to more than 10 depending on field direction [12]), so their frequencies vary a lot.

This number decides your microwave hardware. The QICK firmware runs the 4x2 DACs at 9.8304 GSPS, so the first Nyquist zone ends at about 4.9 GHz (Chapter 19). For a silicon electron spin, 4.9 GHz corresponds to \(B_0 \approx 4.9/28 = 0.175\) T. To drive a silicon qubit at 0.5 T (14 GHz), you need an external mixer and local oscillator to shift the RFSoC's output up in frequency (Chapters 20 and 42).

2.6Rotations: the gates of a single qubit

Any physical evolution of a closed qubit is a unitary matrix \(U\) (one with \(U^\dagger U = I\)). Ignoring global phase, every single-qubit unitary is a rotation of the Bloch sphere. The rotation by angle \(\alpha\) about a unit axis \(\hat n\) is

\[ R_{\hat n}(\alpha) = \exp\!\Big(-i\,\frac{\alpha}{2}\,\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma\Big) = \cos\frac{\alpha}{2}\,I - i\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\,(n_x\sigma_x + n_y\sigma_y + n_z\sigma_z). \]

The second form follows from \((\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma)^2 = I\) and the Taylor series of the exponential. The important special cases have names you will see everywhere:

NameRotationEffect on \(\ket 0\)Typical use
X (or Xπ, "π pulse")180° about x\(\ket 0 \to -i\ket 1\)Flip the spin
X/2 (Xπ/2, "π/2 pulse")90° about x\(\ket 0 \to (\ket 0 - i\ket 1)/\sqrt2\), the −y point on the equatorCreate a superposition (Ramsey, echo)
Y, Y/2180°, 90° about yY/2: \(\ket 0 \to \ket +\)Same as X but with a 90° shifted phase
Z, Z(φ)about zChanges phase onlyOften done "virtually" in software (Chapter 5)
Hadamard H180° about (x+z)/√2\(\ket 0 \to \ket +\)Quantum algorithms; equals Y/2 followed by Z up to phase

One unusual fact: \(R_{\hat n}(2\pi) = -I\). Rotating a spin-1/2 by a full turn gives a minus sign, which is a global phase for one qubit but becomes physical in interference with another system. You need 4π to return exactly to the start. This is a real property of spin-1/2 particles, and it shows up in some two-qubit gate calibrations.

On the 4x2

In Chapter 3 you will see that a microwave burst at the qubit frequency produces a rotation about an axis in the equatorial plane, and the axis angle equals the phase of the microwave. A burst with phase 0° rotates about x; the same burst with phase 90° rotates about y. In QICK this is the phase argument of add_pulse(), with a resolution of \(360°/2^{32}\) [4]. The rotation angle is set by the pulse's amplitude (gain) times its duration. So the two knobs of every single-qubit gate, axis and angle, map directly onto two numbers you type into QICK.

2.7Mixed states and the density matrix

Real experiments never produce a perfectly known pure state. The electron may have been initialised in \(\ket 1\) by mistake 2% of the time, or its phase may have drifted randomly between shots. To describe such statistical mixtures we use the density matrix:

\[ \rho = \sum_k p_k \ket{\psi_k}\bra{\psi_k} = \frac{1}{2}\big(I + r_x\sigma_x + r_y\sigma_y + r_z\sigma_z\big), \qquad |\vec r| \le 1 . \]

The first form says "with probability \(p_k\) the system is in \(\ket{\psi_k}\)". The second form shows that any qubit density matrix is described by a Bloch vector \(\vec r\) whose length can now be less than 1. Pure states lie on the surface; mixed states lie inside; the centre (\(\vec r = 0\), \(\rho = I/2\)) is the completely mixed state, a fair coin with no phase information at all.

Probabilities come from the diagonal: \(P(0) = \rho_{00}\), \(P(1) = \rho_{11}\). The off-diagonal elements \(\rho_{01} = \rho_{10}^*\) are called coherences. They encode the relative phase. Decoherence (Chapter 4) is the process by which coherences shrink to zero and the Bloch vector shrinks towards the z axis.

Worked example: thermal initialisation

If you simply wait for the spin to relax into equilibrium with the electron reservoir at temperature \(T_e\), the excited-state probability is \(P(1) = 1/(1 + e^{E_Z/k_B T_e})\). For a silicon qubit at \(B_0 = 0.5\) T (\(E_Z = 57.9\ \mu\)eV) and an electron temperature of 100 mK (\(k_B T_e = 8.6\ \mu\)eV), \(E_Z/k_BT_e = 6.7\) and \(P(1) \approx 0.0012\). So thermal initialisation is 99.9% pure. At 0.175 T, where the 4x2 could drive a silicon qubit directly, and the same 100 mK, \(E_Z/k_BT_e = 2.4\) and \(P(1) \approx 0.09\): only about 91% pure. This is one reason why low-field operation, which the 4x2 could drive directly, comes with a cost. In practice, spin qubits are usually initialised by spin-selective tunnelling or Pauli blockade rather than by waiting (Chapter 11).

2.8Two qubits, entanglement and the singlet

Two qubits live in a four-dimensional space spanned by the products \(\ket{00}, \ket{01}, \ket{10}, \ket{11}\), where \(\ket{01} = \ket 0 \otimes \ket 1\) means "qubit 1 in \(\ket 0\), qubit 2 in \(\ket 1\)". A general state is

\[ \ket\Psi = c_{00}\ket{00} + c_{01}\ket{01} + c_{10}\ket{10} + c_{11}\ket{11} . \]

If \(\ket\Psi\) can be written as a product \(\ket{\psi_1}\otimes\ket{\psi_2}\), the qubits are independent. If it cannot, they are entangled. The most important entangled state for this book is the spin singlet:

\[ \ket S = \frac{\ket{\uparrow\downarrow} - \ket{\downarrow\uparrow}}{\sqrt 2} . \]

The singlet has total spin zero. The three states with total spin one are the triplets:

\[ \ket{T_+} = \ket{\uparrow\uparrow}, \qquad \ket{T_0} = \frac{\ket{\uparrow\downarrow} + \ket{\downarrow\uparrow}}{\sqrt 2}, \qquad \ket{T_-} = \ket{\downarrow\downarrow}. \]

Two electrons in neighbouring quantum dots naturally form these states, and the energy difference between singlet and triplets, the exchange energy \(J\), is controlled by gate voltages. That one fact underlies the singlet–triplet qubit, the exchange-only qubit, Pauli spin blockade readout and all two-qubit gates between spins (Chapters 11, 13 and 14).

Check yourself

1. Where on the Bloch sphere is the state \((\ket 0 - i\ket 1)/\sqrt 2\)? What is \(P(1)\)?

Show answer
It is \(\cos(\theta/2)=\sin(\theta/2)=1/\sqrt2\), so \(\theta = 90°\) (on the equator), and \(e^{i\varphi} = -i\), so \(\varphi = 270°\) (the −y axis). \(P(1) = 1/2\).

2. A silicon spin qubit is driven at 3.2 GHz. What magnetic field is applied?

Show answer
\(B_0 = f_0/(28.0\ \text{GHz/T}) = 3.2/28.0 \approx 0.114\) T (assuming \(g = 2.00\)). In a micromagnet device, the micromagnet adds its own field component along \(B_0\), so the applied field would be somewhat lower.

3. You measure \(P(1) = 0.5\) for a state. Can you tell whether it is \(\ket +\), \(\ket{+i}\) or the completely mixed state? What would you do?

Show answer
Not from a z measurement alone: all three give 50/50. Rotate before measuring. A rotation of −90° about y takes the +x axis to +z, so \(\ket +\) then gives 0 every time. A rotation of +90° about x takes +y to +z, so \(\ket{+i}\) then gives 0 every time. The completely mixed state stays 50/50 whatever rotation you apply. This is state tomography.

4. Why do we need 2500 shots for 1% precision near \(P = 0.5\) but only about 200 near \(P = 0.02\)?

Show answer
The binomial variance \(P(1-P)\) is largest at \(P = 0.5\) (0.25) and small near 0 or 1 (0.0196 at \(P=0.02\)). \(N = P(1-P)/\sigma^2 = 0.0196/10^{-4} \approx 196\).
Summary
  • A qubit state is \(a\ket0 + b\ket1\) with complex amplitudes; measurement gives 0 or 1 with probabilities \(|a|^2\) and \(|b|^2\), so experiments are repeated over many shots.
  • Dropping the global phase, every pure state is a point on the Bloch sphere: latitude sets probabilities, longitude is the relative phase.
  • In a field \(B_0\) the spin precesses about z at \(f_0 = |g|\mu_B B_0/h\): 28 GHz/T for silicon electrons, 6.2 GHz/T for GaAs.
  • Gates are rotations \(R_{\hat n}(\alpha)\); a microwave burst's phase sets the rotation axis and its area sets the angle.
  • Mixed states have Bloch vectors inside the sphere; decoherence shrinks them.
  • Two spins form singlet and triplet states, split by the exchange energy \(J\).

Part I · Quantum mechanics you need · Chapter 3

Driving a qubit: resonance, Rabi oscillations and the rotating frame

Why you need this

Almost every single-qubit operation is a burst of oscillating field at (or near) the qubit frequency. The first coherent experiment on any new qubit is a Rabi oscillation: you drive the spin for a variable time and watch \(P(1)\) swing up and down. To set up that experiment you must understand what controls the swing's speed (drive amplitude), what happens off resonance (detuning), why the drive's phase picks the rotation axis, and why physicists talk about a "rotating frame". These ideas then define your calibrations: π-pulse length, qubit frequency, pulse shape.

A spin in a static field just precesses. To make it change latitude, that is, to flip it, we must push it with a second, oscillating field. The push only works if it keeps in step with the precession. This chapter makes that statement exact.

3.1The picture: pushing a swing

Imagine pushing a child on a swing. If you push once per swing, always at the same point, the swing goes higher and higher. If you push at a slightly different rate, sometimes your push helps and sometimes it fights the motion, so the amplitude grows, then shrinks, then grows again. That is resonance and detuning.

A spin precessing at \(f_0\) around z behaves similarly. A small oscillating magnetic field \(B_1\) perpendicular to z gives the spin a tiny torque. If \(B_1\) oscillates at \(f_0\), the torque always points the same way relative to the precessing spin, so its effect accumulates and the spin slowly tips over from the north pole towards the south pole and back. This slow tipping is the Rabi oscillation, at a frequency \(f_R\) much lower than \(f_0\). For spin qubits \(f_0\) is GHz and \(f_R\) is typically 1–20 MHz.

3.2The driven Hamiltonian

Add an oscillating transverse term to the Zeeman Hamiltonian of Chapter 2:

\[ H(t) = \frac{\hbar\omega_0}{2}\,\sigma_z + \hbar\Omega\cos(\omega t + \phi)\,\sigma_x . \]

Here \(\omega = 2\pi f\) is the drive frequency (what you set on your generator), \(\phi\) is the drive phase, and \(\Omega\) is proportional to the drive amplitude. For true electron spin resonance (ESR), where a real oscillating magnetic field \(B_1\cos(\omega t+\phi)\) is applied along x, \(\hbar\Omega = \tfrac12 g\mu_B B_1\). For electric-dipole spin resonance (EDSR) with a micromagnet (Chapter 12), an oscillating electric field moves the electron in a field gradient and produces the same mathematical term with a different constant.

3.3Going to the rotating frame

The time dependence of \(H(t)\) makes the Schrödinger equation hard to solve directly. The standard trick is to look at the spin from a reference frame that itself rotates around z at the drive frequency \(\omega\). Imagine standing on a merry-go-round turning at \(\omega\). A spin precessing at exactly \(\omega_0 = \omega\) then looks stationary, and the oscillating drive looks like a constant field.

Mathematically, define \(\ket{\tilde\psi} = U\ket\psi\) with \(U(t) = e^{i\omega t\sigma_z/2}\). Substituting into the Schrödinger equation gives a new effective Hamiltonian

\[ \tilde H = U H U^\dagger + i\hbar\,\dot U U^\dagger . \]

Two identities do the work. First, \(i\hbar\dot UU^\dagger = -\tfrac{\hbar\omega}{2}\sigma_z\), which subtracts the frame's rotation. Second, rotating \(\sigma_x\) about z gives \(U\sigma_xU^\dagger = \sigma_x\cos\omega t - \sigma_y\sin\omega t\). Using the product formulas \(\cos A\cos B = \tfrac12[\cos(A-B) + \cos(A+B)]\) and \(\cos A\sin B = \tfrac12[\sin(A+B) - \sin(A-B)]\), the drive term becomes

\[ \begin{aligned} \hbar\Omega\cos(\omega t+\phi)\big(\sigma_x\cos\omega t - \sigma_y\sin\omega t\big) &= \frac{\hbar\Omega}{2}\big(\cos\phi\,\sigma_x + \sin\phi\,\sigma_y\big) \\ &\quad + \frac{\hbar\Omega}{2}\big(\cos(2\omega t+\phi)\,\sigma_x - \sin(2\omega t+\phi)\,\sigma_y\big). \end{aligned} \]

The second line oscillates at twice the drive frequency. Because \(\Omega \ll \omega\) (MHz versus GHz), its effect averages to nearly zero over any time scale where the spin moves appreciably. Dropping it is the rotating-wave approximation (RWA). The result is a time-independent Hamiltonian:

\[ \boxed{\;\tilde H = \frac{\hbar\Delta}{2}\,\sigma_z + \frac{\hbar\Omega}{2}\big(\cos\phi\,\sigma_x + \sin\phi\,\sigma_y\big),\qquad \Delta = \omega_0 - \omega\;} \]

This one equation contains almost everything about single-qubit control:

  • \(\Delta\) is the detuning. On resonance \(\Delta = 0\) and only the drive term remains.
  • The drive term is a rotation about an axis in the equatorial plane at angle \(\phi\) from x. The phase of your microwave chooses the rotation axis.
  • \(\Omega\) is the Rabi frequency (in angular units); \(f_R = \Omega/2\pi\).

Since \(\tilde H = \tfrac{\hbar}{2}\vec W\cdot\vec\sigma\) with \(\vec W = (\Omega\cos\phi, \Omega\sin\phi, \Delta)\), the evolution is a rotation (Chapter 2) about the axis \(\hat n = \vec W/|\vec W|\) at angular speed

\[ W = \sqrt{\Omega^2 + \Delta^2}, \]

called the generalised Rabi frequency.

3.4The Rabi formula

Starting in \(\ket 0\) and driving for a time \(t\), the probability of finding \(\ket 1\) follows from rotating the north pole about \(\hat n\) by angle \(Wt\):

\[ P_1(t) = \frac{\Omega^2}{\Omega^2 + \Delta^2}\,\sin^2\!\Big(\frac{\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}}{2}\,t\Big). \]

Check the limits. On resonance, \(P_1 = \sin^2(\Omega t/2)\): the spin is fully flipped at \(t_\pi = \pi/\Omega = 1/(2f_R)\). Far off resonance (\(|\Delta| \gg \Omega\)), the amplitude \(\Omega^2/\Delta^2\) is tiny and the oscillation is fast: the drive barely affects the spin.

If you sweep both the drive time and the drive frequency, you get a 2D map called a Rabi chevron, named after its V-shaped pattern. It is one of the most useful plots in qubit tune-up: the centre line gives the exact qubit frequency, and the period along that line gives the π time.

Worked example: pulse times

Your Rabi oscillation on resonance has a period of 400 ns, so \(f_R = 2.5\) MHz.

  • π pulse (X): \(t_\pi = 1/(2f_R) = 200\) ns.
  • π/2 pulse (X/2): 100 ns.
  • If you double the drive amplitude (and the drive is linear), \(f_R\) doubles to 5 MHz and \(t_\pi\) halves to 100 ns.

Real silicon EDSR qubits reach \(f_R\) from below 1 MHz to around 10–20 MHz depending on micromagnet design and drive power [13, 7]. Faster is better for gate speed, but strong drive heats the device and can shift the qubit frequency, so labs choose a compromise.

3.5Pulse area, pulse shapes and why shapes matter

On resonance, the rotation angle depends only on the integral of the drive envelope. If the drive amplitude changes in time, \(\Omega(t)\), the rotation angle is the pulse area

\[ \alpha = \int \Omega(t)\,dt . \]

A π pulse can therefore be short and strong or long and weak, square or Gaussian, as long as the area is π. In practice square pulses are rarely ideal. A sharp edge contains a wide range of frequencies (Chapter 21), which can excite unwanted transitions, for example a neighbouring qubit only a few MHz away, or a higher valley state. Smooth envelopes such as Gaussians, cosine ramps or flat-top pulses keep the spectrum narrow. For a Gaussian envelope of width \(\sigma\), the spectral width is about \(1/(2\pi\sigma)\).

On the 4x2

QICK provides three pulse styles: const (square), arb (any envelope you upload, for example a Gaussian from add_gauss()), and flat_top (envelope halves for the edges, constant middle) [4]. On the 4x2, the envelope memory per generator holds 65 536 complex samples, which at 9.8304 GSPS is about 6.7 µs of arbitrary waveform. Constant and flat-top pulses can be much longer because their middle part is not stored sample by sample [3].

3.6Frequency-domain view: spectroscopy

Instead of sweeping time, you can fix the pulse (say a π pulse calibrated on resonance) and sweep the drive frequency. This is pulsed spectroscopy. From the Rabi formula with \(\Omega t = \pi\):

\[ P_1(\Delta) = \frac{\Omega^2}{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}\sin^2\!\Big(\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{1+\Delta^2/\Omega^2}\Big). \]

The central peak has a full width of roughly \(1.6\,\Omega/2\pi\), about 1.6 times the Rabi frequency. That gives a rule of thumb: to find an unknown resonance quickly, drive hard (wide line, easy to hit) and then reduce power to locate it precisely.

With a long, weak, continuous drive, the line width is instead set by decoherence. In the steady state of the Bloch equations (Chapter 4) the line is a Lorentzian of half-width

\[ \Delta\omega_{1/2} = \frac{1}{T_2}\sqrt{1 + \Omega^2 T_1 T_2}, \]

which grows with drive strength. This growth is called power broadening. When you see a broad line, lower the power until the width stops shrinking; that limiting width tells you about \(T_2^*\).

In the lab

The first time a group finds an EDSR resonance on a new device, they usually do a 2D scan of drive frequency against magnetic field with a long, strong burst. The resonance appears as a straight line \(f_0 = g\mu_B (B_0 + B_{\text{mm}})/h\) whose slope gives the g-factor and whose offset reveals the micromagnet's field \(B_{\text{mm}}\) at the dot. Two dots under one micromagnet show two parallel lines separated by the field difference between them, typically tens to hundreds of MHz, which is what makes individual addressing possible (Chapter 12).

3.7When the rotating-wave approximation fails

The RWA needs \(\Omega \ll \omega_0\). For spin qubits (MHz Rabi, GHz qubit frequency) this is extremely well satisfied. The leading correction, the Bloch–Siegert shift, moves the resonance by about \(\Omega^2/(4\omega_0)\): for \(f_R = 10\) MHz and \(f_0 = 10\) GHz that is 2.5 kHz, usually negligible but measurable in precise experiments. Two related effects matter more in practice:

  • AC Stark (light) shifts: a strong drive on one transition shifts nearby transitions. When two qubits share a drive line, the drive for qubit A shifts qubit B's frequency and adds phase errors that must be calibrated [14, 15].
  • Heating-induced frequency shifts: in silicon EDSR devices, strong microwave power warms the device and shifts qubit frequencies by up to MHz. Labs often apply a constant "pre-pulse" or keep the average power fixed to stabilise this [16].

3.8Phase, frames and keeping track of time

In the rotating frame we measure angles relative to the drive. That means the phase of your drive generator is your reference clock for the qubit. Two consequences matter a lot when you program the hardware:

  1. Phase coherence. Every pulse in a sequence must have a well-defined phase relative to the same continuously running reference at frequency \(\omega\). If the generator's phase jumps randomly between pulses, a Ramsey experiment shows no fringes even for a perfect qubit. QICK's signal generators use a phase accumulator that keeps running between pulses (it can be reset on request), so pulses at the same frequency stay phase coherent [3].
  2. Virtual Z gates. A rotation about z is just a phase shift. Instead of applying it physically, you can add its angle to the phase of every following drive pulse. This "virtual Z" is exact and takes zero time. Most spin-qubit groups implement Z gates this way (Chapter 5).
Common mistake

Changing the drive frequency between pulses, for instance to address two qubits with one generator, breaks the simple phase picture: the rotating frame of qubit A is not that of qubit B. Each qubit needs its own phase bookkeeping, as if it had its own oscillator. With QICK you either dedicate one generator per qubit frequency, or keep careful track of the accumulated phase \(2\pi\,\delta f\,t\) yourself. Multiplexed generators (several tones on one output) exist in QICK firmware for larger boards, but the 4x2's standard firmware has two full-speed generators [3].

Check yourself

1. A Rabi oscillation reaches only \(P_1 = 0.5\) at its maximum, with perfect readout. What is \(|\Delta|/\Omega\)?

Show answer
The amplitude is \(\Omega^2/(\Omega^2+\Delta^2) = 0.5\), so \(\Delta^2 = \Omega^2\) and \(|\Delta| = \Omega\). The drive is detuned by one Rabi frequency.

2. You play an X/2 pulse with phase 0°, then the same pulse with phase 180°. What is the net operation?

Show answer
The second pulse rotates about −x by 90°, which undoes the first. The net operation is the identity (up to global phase). This makes a good calibration check: any residual signal shows amplitude or phase errors.

3. Why does a weaker drive give a narrower spectroscopy line?

Show answer
The width of the pulsed resonance scales with \(\Omega\); the drive only acts strongly when \(|\Delta| \lesssim \Omega\). With weaker drive (and a correspondingly longer pulse), only frequencies closer to the resonance produce a full flip, until the width reaches the limit set by decoherence and frequency fluctuations.
Summary
  • A transverse field oscillating at \(\omega\) near \(\omega_0\) drives Rabi oscillations; in the rotating frame (RWA) the Hamiltonian is \(\tfrac{\hbar}{2}(\Delta\sigma_z + \Omega\cos\phi\,\sigma_x + \Omega\sin\phi\,\sigma_y)\).
  • The drive phase \(\phi\) sets the rotation axis; the pulse area \(\int\Omega\,dt\) sets the angle; detuning tilts the axis.
  • \(P_1(t) = \frac{\Omega^2}{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}\sin^2(\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}\,t/2)\); a Rabi chevron maps this in time and frequency.
  • Smooth pulse shapes reduce spectral leakage; spectroscopy line width shrinks with drive power until decoherence sets the limit.
  • The drive generator's phase is the qubit's reference clock, so phase coherence and phase bookkeeping (virtual Z) are essential.

Part I · Quantum mechanics you need · Chapter 4

Decoherence and noise: T1, T2*, T2 and noise spectra

Why you need this

A qubit is only useful while it remembers its state. The three numbers every spin-qubit paper reports, \(T_1\), \(T_2^*\) and \(T_2\), measure how long that memory lasts against different kinds of disturbance. Measuring them is among the first experiments on any new device, and the ratio of coherence time to gate time decides how good your gates can be. This chapter explains what each number means physically, how each is measured with a pulse sequence you will program on the RFSoC, and how the noise environment of a semiconductor device sets them.

In Chapters 2 and 3 the qubit was perfectly isolated. A real spin in a real device is surrounded by fluctuating electric fields from charge traps, nuclear spins in the crystal, lattice vibrations (phonons) and noise coming down your control wires. Each of these slowly scrambles the qubit's state. "Decoherence" is the umbrella word for this scrambling.

4.1Two different ways to lose information

Look at the Bloch vector again. It can lose information in two distinct ways:

  1. Energy relaxation. The spin flips from \(\ket 1\) (higher energy) to \(\ket 0\) by giving its energy \(E_Z\) to the environment, usually a phonon. The Bloch vector's z component relaxes towards the ground state. The time scale is \(T_1\).
  2. Dephasing. The qubit frequency fluctuates slightly, so the phase \(\varphi\) drifts by an unknown amount. Averaged over many shots, Bloch vectors pointing in different directions around the equator cancel each other, and the transverse (x, y) components shrink to zero. No energy is exchanged. The time scale is \(T_2\) (or \(T_2^*\), see below).

Both appear in the Bloch equations, written in the rotating frame without drive:

\[ \frac{dr_z}{dt} = -\frac{r_z - r_z^{\text{eq}}}{T_1}, \qquad \frac{dr_{x,y}}{dt} = -\frac{r_{x,y}}{T_2} . \]

Because relaxation also destroys phase information, the two times always satisfy \(T_2 \le 2T_1\). For spin qubits in silicon, \(T_1\) is usually much longer than \(T_2\) (milliseconds to seconds versus microseconds), so in practice dephasing is the dominant problem [7].

4.2T1: energy relaxation

Measurement

The T1 measurement is the simplest sequence there is:

initialise |0⟩ → X (π pulse) → wait τ → measure

Sweep \(\tau\) and fit \(P_1(\tau) = A\,e^{-\tau/T_1} + B\). The constants \(A\) and \(B\) absorb imperfect initialisation and readout; never force them to 1 and 0.

For spin qubits there is a cheaper way that does not need a calibrated π pulse at all. Load an electron with a random spin from the reservoir and read it out after a variable delay (Chapter 11). This is how the first spin T1 values were measured, years before coherent control was possible [17].

What sets T1 for a spin in a dot

A phonon cannot flip a spin directly: phonons are lattice vibrations that couple to charge, not to spin. Relaxation happens because spin–orbit coupling slightly mixes spin and orbital states, so the "spin-up" state contains a small admixture of an excited orbital (or, in silicon, valley) state that phonons can couple to. The resulting rates grow steeply with magnetic field, roughly as \(B^5\) for the common phonon mechanism, so T1 can be seconds at low field and milliseconds at higher field [18, 8]. In silicon, T1 drops sharply near a "hot spot" where the Zeeman energy equals the valley splitting (Chapter 10), because there the spin and valley states mix strongly. Measuring T1 versus field is therefore a standard way to measure the valley splitting of a device.

On the 4x2

Long waits are easy for QICK: the tProcessor's time values are 32-bit integers in units of its clock (about 2.4 ns on the 4x2's tProc v1 firmware, 409.6 MHz), so a single wait can last up to \(2^{31}\times 2.44\ \text{ns} \approx 5\) s, and loops extend that further [4]. For T1 sweeps, use a logarithmic list of delays: the interesting range often spans µs to s.

4.3T2*: dephasing from slow fluctuations

The Ramsey experiment

The Ramsey experiment measures how long the phase survives. It uses two π/2 pulses separated by a free-evolution time \(\tau\):

initialise |0⟩ → X/2 → wait τ → X/2 → measure

Follow it on the Bloch sphere. The first X/2 puts the vector on the equator (at −y). During \(\tau\) it precesses in the rotating frame at the detuning \(\Delta\), picking up phase \(\Delta\tau\). The second X/2 rotates the equator back onto the z axis, so the final \(P_1\) depends on where the vector had moved to:

\[ P_1(\tau) = \tfrac12\big[1 + \cos(\Delta\tau)\big] \quad\text{(no noise)}. \]

These oscillations are Ramsey fringes. Their frequency equals the detuning, which makes Ramsey the most precise way to measure the qubit frequency. In practice you deliberately detune by a few MHz to see fringes clearly.

Why the fringes decay

Now suppose the qubit frequency is slightly different on every shot because of slow noise, by an amount \(\delta\omega\) drawn from a Gaussian distribution of width \(\sigma\). Each shot gives \(\cos((\Delta+\delta\omega)\tau)\), and averaging over the Gaussian gives

\[ \ev{\cos((\Delta+\delta\omega)\tau)} = e^{-\sigma^2\tau^2/2}\cos(\Delta\tau) . \]

So the fringes decay as a Gaussian, \(P_1 = \tfrac12[1 + e^{-(\tau/T_2^*)^2}\cos\Delta\tau]\), with

\[ T_2^* = \frac{\sqrt 2}{\sigma} . \]

The star marks this as the inhomogeneous dephasing time. It is not really a property of the spin alone but of the spin plus everything that drifted during your averaging. It depends on how long you average: integrate for an hour instead of a minute and slow drifts make \(T_2^*\) shorter.

Worked example

A silicon qubit has \(T_2^* = 2\ \mu\)s. What spread of qubit frequencies does that imply?

\(\sigma = \sqrt2/T_2^* = 1.41/(2\times10^{-6}) = 7.1\times10^5\) rad/s, or \(\sigma/2\pi \approx 113\) kHz. The qubit frequency (around 10 GHz) is wandering by about 100 kHz, about one part in \(10^5\). For a qubit in a micromagnet gradient of 0.3 mT/nm (8.4 MHz/nm at 28 GHz/T), that corresponds to the electron moving by only about 13 picometres along the gradient. This is how sensitive these qubits are, and why charge noise matters so much in micromagnet devices.

Typical numbers

PlatformMain dephasing sourceTypical \(T_2^*\)
GaAs electron spinHyperfine coupling to ~106 Ga and As nuclear spins~10–20 ns [19, 18]
Natural Si/SiGe (4.7% 29Si)29Si nuclear spins, charge noise~1 µs [20]
Isotopically purified 28Si/SiGe (800 ppm 29Si)Charge noise through the micromagnet gradient~20 µs [13]

The jump from nanoseconds in GaAs to tens of microseconds in purified silicon is the single biggest reason the field moved to silicon. Every Ga and As nucleus carries spin, but silicon's only spinful isotope, 29Si, can be removed.

4.4T2: the Hahn echo and dynamical decoupling

Much of the noise behind \(T_2^*\) is slow: the qubit frequency is different from shot to shot, but nearly constant within one shot. Such quasi-static noise can be undone. Insert a π pulse halfway through the free evolution:

X/2 → wait τ/2 → X (π) → wait τ/2 → X/2 → measure

In the first half, an unknown detuning \(\delta\omega\) adds phase \(+\delta\omega\tau/2\). The π pulse flips the vector to the other side of the sphere, which reverses the sign of the accumulated phase. In the second half the same \(\delta\omega\) adds another \(+\delta\omega\tau/2\), which now cancels the first half exactly. This is the Hahn echo. The decay that remains is caused by noise that changes during the sequence, and its time scale is called \(T_2\) (or \(T_2^{\text{Hahn}}\)).

Analogy

Runners of slightly different speeds start together. After a while they are spread out. If everyone turns around at the same moment and runs back at the same speed, they all arrive at the start line together. That is the echo. It fails only if a runner's speed changes during the race.

Adding more π pulses (Carr–Purcell–Meiboom–Gill, or CPMG, sequences, and other dynamical decoupling schemes) cancels noise up to higher frequencies. In purified silicon, decoupling extends coherence from tens of microseconds to milliseconds [7]. In GaAs, echo extends coherence from about 10 ns to about 1 µs or more [19].

4.5Noise spectra and filter functions

To understand which sequence protects against which noise, describe the noise by its power spectral density (PSD) \(S(f)\). Write the instantaneous qubit-frequency fluctuation as \(\delta\omega(t)\). The PSD tells you how much of its variance comes from each frequency: \(\ev{\delta\omega^2} = \int_0^\infty S(f)\,df\) (a one-sided PSD).

A pulse sequence is summarised by a sign function \(y(t)\), equal to +1 or −1 depending on how many π pulses have been applied so far. The phase accumulated in one shot is \(\varphi = \int_0^\tau y(t)\,\delta\omega(t)\,dt\). For Gaussian noise, the remaining coherence is \(e^{-\ev{\varphi^2}/2}\), and a short calculation gives

\[ \ev{\varphi^2} = \int_0^\infty S(f)\,\big|Y(f)\big|^2\,df, \qquad Y(f) = \int_0^\tau y(t)\,e^{-i2\pi f t}\,dt . \]

\(|Y(f)|^2\) is the sequence's filter function. For Ramsey, \(y = 1\) throughout and \(|Y|^2 = \sin^2(\pi f\tau)/(\pi f)^2\), which is largest at \(f = 0\): Ramsey is most sensitive to the slowest noise. For the echo, \(|Y|^2 = 16\sin^4(\pi f\tau/2)/(2\pi f)^2\), which vanishes at \(f = 0\): the echo is blind to static noise and most sensitive near \(f\approx 1/\tau\). CPMG with \(N\) pulses moves the sensitivity peak to \(f \approx N/(2\tau)\). By measuring decay with different \(N\), you can reconstruct \(S(f)\) itself. This is noise spectroscopy.

1/f charge noise: the main enemy in silicon

In silicon devices the dominant noise is usually 1/f noise from charge traps in the oxide and at interfaces: each trap randomly captures and releases an electron, making a small telegraph signal, and many traps with a wide range of switching rates add up to a spectrum close to \(1/f\). Charge noise moves the dot's electrostatic potential, which moves the electron slightly. Through the micromagnet's field gradient and the Stark shift of the g-factor, that motion becomes qubit-frequency noise. Typical charge-noise amplitudes, referred to the dot's energy, are about 0.1–2 µeV/\(\sqrt{\text{Hz}}\) at 1 Hz in Si/SiGe devices [7, 13].

In the lab

Three practical facts follow from 1/f noise:

  • Recalibrate often. The qubit frequency drifts over minutes to hours. Groups re-measure it with a quick Ramsey every few minutes, or track it with fast real-time feedback.
  • Interleave and randomise. Taking data points in random order, or interleaving reference measurements, prevents slow drifts from looking like a physical effect. The spinQICK exchange-only experiments took a reference measurement before every single shot for this reason [11].
  • Your electronics are part of the noise. Noise on DC gate voltages, on fast pulse lines, or in amplifiers adds directly to charge noise. The HRL spinQICK study used the qubit itself to identify high-frequency noise added by its room-temperature pulse amplifiers [11].
On the 4x2

The FPGA can do more than play fixed sequences. Because it processes readout in real time, it can estimate the qubit frequency from a burst of fast Ramsey shots and update the drive frequency before the next experiment. Real-time estimation and feedback like this is an active research area, and it is a natural use of an RFSoC. A recent example used an FPGA-based controller to keep a silicon double dot's operating point stable against 1/f drift using fast reflectometry [21]. Chapter 44 discusses how to do this with QICK's conditional logic.

Check yourself

1. You measure \(T_2^* = 1\ \mu\)s and \(T_2^{\text{Hahn}} = 50\ \mu\)s. What does the large ratio tell you about the noise?

Show answer
Most of the dephasing comes from slow (quasi-static) noise, which the echo refocuses. Only a small part of the noise power lies near \(1/\tau \approx 20\) kHz. This is typical for 1/f charge noise or nuclear-spin noise.

2. Why does a Ramsey experiment with no deliberate detuning look like a simple decay rather than oscillations?

Show answer
With \(\Delta = 0\), \(\cos(\Delta\tau) = 1\), so only the envelope is visible. A small residual detuning gives a slow oscillation that can be mistaken for decay. Deliberately detuning by several \(1/T_2^*\) makes the fringes clear and gives both the frequency and the decay.

3. Can \(T_2\) be longer than \(2T_1\)? Why or why not?

Show answer
No. Energy relaxation also destroys the coherences: the off-diagonal density-matrix elements decay at least at rate \(1/(2T_1)\). So \(1/T_2 = 1/(2T_1) + 1/T_\phi \ge 1/(2T_1)\), where \(T_\phi\) is the pure dephasing time.
Summary
  • \(T_1\): energy relaxation; measure with π – wait – read. For spins it is long (ms–s) and set by spin–orbit/valley-mediated phonon processes.
  • \(T_2^*\): dephasing from slow frequency fluctuations; measure with Ramsey (X/2 – wait – X/2); Gaussian decay \(e^{-(\tau/T_2^*)^2}\).
  • \(T_2\): coherence after refocusing; Hahn echo and dynamical decoupling cancel slow noise.
  • Filter functions show which noise frequencies each sequence is sensitive to; 1/f charge noise dominates silicon devices.
  • GaAs: \(T_2^*\sim 10\) ns (nuclei). Natural Si: ~1 µs. Purified 28Si: ~20 µs.

Part I · Quantum mechanics you need · Chapter 5

Gates, measurement and fidelity

Why you need this

Research groups are judged by numbers like "99.9% single-qubit gate fidelity", "98% readout fidelity" or "two-qubit gate above the fault-tolerance threshold". To read those papers, and to produce such numbers yourself, you need to know what a gate set is, how gate errors and readout errors are separated, and how techniques like randomised benchmarking work. These experiments also put the hardest demands on your control electronics: long random pulse sequences, exact phase bookkeeping and many repetitions.

5.1What a gate set is

A quantum computation is a sequence of gates. A small set of gates is universal if combinations of them can approximate any operation. A standard universal set is: arbitrary single-qubit rotations plus one entangling two-qubit gate such as CNOT or CZ.

In spin-qubit experiments the physical single-qubit gates are usually just two: X/2 and Y/2 (π/2 rotations about x and y), made with microwave bursts at phases 0° and 90°. All other single-qubit rotations are built from these plus Z rotations:

  • Virtual Z. A Z(θ) rotation is implemented by adding θ to the phase of every later drive pulse on that qubit. It costs no time and has no error. A Y/2 is then the same burst as X/2 with a phase shift, and an arbitrary rotation \(U = Z(\alpha)\,X/2\,Z(\beta)\,X/2\,Z(\gamma)\) needs only two physical pulses.
  • Composite sequences. X = X/2·X/2; Hadamard ≈ Y/2 followed by Z(π).

The most common two-qubit gates for spins (Chapter 14) are:

GateMatrix (basis 00, 01, 10, 11)How spins do it
CZ (controlled phase)diag(1, 1, 1, −1)Pulse the exchange \(J\) on for a calibrated time (adiabatically)
CNOT / CROTFlip target if control is 1Exchange on + a frequency-selective microwave pulse that only flips one target-qubit transition
SWAP, √SWAPExchange the two statesLarge exchange pulse, when \(J\) dominates the Zeeman difference

5.2Fidelity: how close to perfect is "close"?

The fidelity between an ideal pure state \(\ket\psi\) and the actual state \(\rho\) is \(F = \bra\psi\rho\ket\psi\), the probability that the actual state would pass a test for being \(\ket\psi\). For a gate, the average gate fidelity averages this over all possible input states. The error per gate is \(r = 1 - F\).

A useful rule of thumb links gate error to coherence: during a gate of duration \(t_g\) the qubit dephases by roughly \(t_g/T_2\) (using the coherence time that applies during driving, which is often close to the echo \(T_2\) because driving itself refocuses slow noise). So

\[ r \sim \frac{t_g}{T_2} . \]
Worked example

A purified silicon qubit with \(T_2 \approx 50\ \mu\)s and an X/2 gate of 50 ns: \(r \sim 50\times10^{-9}/50\times10^{-6} = 10^{-3}\), so \(F \sim 99.9\%\). This matches the level reported in the best single-spin silicon experiments [13]. A GaAs spin with \(T_2^* = 15\) ns and the same 50 ns gate would be hopeless without decoupling, which is why GaAs experiments relied on fast exchange-based singlet–triplet control.

Why do we care about 99% versus 99.9%? Because quantum error correction only works when the physical error per operation is below a threshold. For the widely studied surface code the threshold is around 1% per operation; operating well below it (0.1%) makes error correction efficient. Silicon spin qubits crossed 99% two-qubit fidelity in 2022 in three independent groups [14, 15, 22].

5.3Measurement: readout fidelity and SPAM

Measurement in a spin-qubit device is indirect: the spin is converted to a charge state, the charge state changes a sensor's signal, and the signal is integrated over a readout window. Each shot gives one number (or an I/Q pair, Chapter 23). The shots from \(\ket 0\) and from \(\ket 1\) form two distributions, usually close to Gaussian, separated by some distance and each with a width set by noise.

Assign 0 below the threshold and 1 above. The two error probabilities are \(\epsilon_0 = P(\text{read }1\,|\,0)\) and \(\epsilon_1 = P(\text{read }0\,|\,1)\), and the readout fidelity is usually quoted as

\[ F_{\text{RO}} = 1 - \frac{\epsilon_0 + \epsilon_1}{2} \quad\text{or the visibility}\quad V = 1 - \epsilon_0 - \epsilon_1 . \]

For two Gaussians of equal width \(\sigma\) separated by \(\Delta\mu\), define the signal-to-noise ratio \(\text{SNR} = \Delta\mu/\sigma\). With the threshold in the middle, each error is \(\epsilon = \tfrac12\operatorname{erfc}\!\big(\text{SNR}/(2\sqrt2)\big)\).

SNR (Δµ/σ)2468
Error per state15.9%2.3%0.13%0.003%

Integrating longer improves SNR as \(\sqrt{t_{\text{int}}}\) for white noise, but the spin may relax during the window, so there is an optimum integration time. Chapter 23 shows how to choose it and how the FPGA computes it in real time. The spinQICK exchange-only work reports SNR values of 5–6 [11].

Initialisation is also imperfect. Errors in state preparation and measurement are lumped together as SPAM errors. They are why every curve in Chapter 4 needed a free amplitude and offset, and why gate characterisation methods are designed to be insensitive to them.

5.4Calibration sequences: AllXY

Before measuring fidelities you need well-calibrated pulses. A favourite quick check is AllXY: 21 short sequences of two pulses each (for example XX, YY, XY, X/2 Y/2, …) chosen so that ideal results form a staircase of 0, ½ and 1. Each kind of error (wrong amplitude, wrong detuning, wrong phase between x and y) distorts the staircase in a characteristic way, so one glance tells you what to fix. spinQICK includes AllXY for single-spin qubits [10].

5.5Randomised benchmarking

How do you measure a 0.1% gate error when readout errors are 2%? Randomised benchmarking (RB) solves this:

  1. Choose a random sequence of \(m\) gates from the Clifford group (24 operations for one qubit).
  2. Append the one Clifford that inverts the whole sequence, so that the ideal final state is \(\ket 0\).
  3. Measure the probability of getting 0. Average over many random sequences of the same length.
  4. Repeat for many lengths \(m\) and fit \(P(m) = A\,p^m + B\).

SPAM errors only affect \(A\) and \(B\), not the decay constant \(p\). Random sequences turn coherent errors into an average depolarising effect, so the decay is a clean exponential. The average error per Clifford is \(r = (1-p)(d-1)/d\), with \(d = 2\) for one qubit. If each Clifford is built from on average 1.875 physical X/2 or Y/2 pulses, the error per physical gate is about \(r/1.875\).

Variants you will see in papers: interleaved RB (insert one specific gate between random Cliffords to measure that gate's error), two-qubit RB (Cliffords on two qubits, much longer sequences), and gate set tomography (GST), which reconstructs the full error model of every gate and was used in several of the 2022 silicon threshold papers [14, 22].

On the 4x2

RB is a demanding test of a controller. You need hundreds of different random sequences, each up to hundreds of gates long, with exact phase tracking. With QICK, two strategies work:

  • Compile each random sequence into its own short QICK program and run them one after another from Python. Simple, but loading many programs adds overhead.
  • Store the Clifford pulses once and let the tProcessor select them in a loop from a table in data memory. tProc v2 programs are limited to about 4096 instructions [4], so long sequences must be built with loops and table look-ups rather than written out.

Virtual Z gates are implemented in QICK by changing the phase parameter of following pulses, which costs no time.

Check yourself

1. Your readout histograms are separated by 3σ. Roughly what readout fidelity do you expect, and how much longer would you have to integrate (white noise, no relaxation) to reach SNR 6?

Show answer
Error per state is \(\tfrac12\operatorname{erfc}(3/2.83) \approx 6.7\%\), so \(F_{RO}\approx 93\%\). SNR grows as \(\sqrt{t}\), so doubling SNR needs 4 times the integration time.

2. Why is RB insensitive to SPAM errors?

Show answer
SPAM errors happen once per sequence, regardless of its length. They change the overall scale and offset (\(A\), \(B\)) but not how fast the signal decays with the number of gates \(m\), which is what gives the gate error.

3. A Rabi frequency of 5 MHz gives what X/2 duration? With \(T_2 = 30\ \mu\)s, estimate the gate fidelity limit.

Show answer
\(t_{X/2} = 1/(4f_R) = 50\) ns. \(r \sim 50\text{ ns}/30\ \mu\text{s} \approx 1.7\times10^{-3}\), so \(F\approx 99.8\%\).
Summary
  • Spin qubits typically use physical X/2 and Y/2 pulses, virtual Z gates, and an exchange-based CZ or CROT as the entangling gate.
  • Gate error scales roughly as gate time over coherence time; 1% is the surface-code threshold scale, silicon spins have reached 99.9% (one qubit) and over 99% (two qubits).
  • Readout fidelity follows from histogram overlap; SNR 6 gives about 0.1% error per state.
  • AllXY diagnoses calibration errors; randomised benchmarking measures gate errors independent of SPAM.
